doc.title: Tom McIntosh — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: New York scene: Mingus, Flanagan, Moody, Quincy
title: Quincy calls him uncommercial
summary: Quincy told people Mac was a great composer but the most uncommercial one he knew, and McIntosh agrees, saying he wrote for Miles, Dizzy and Coltrane.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: McIntosh is here. Anything that I do, you have to have them on the same show.” So I was appearing on all kinds of stuff. I remember some students were asking, “Well then what do you do?” So, I went into how I go about composing music for film. Quincy says, “McIntosh, who did you study with?” That’s my Quincy Jones story. And what’s interesting, he told the world, all his associates. He didn’t know that I knew. He said, “Yeah, Mac’s a great composer, but he is the most un-commercial composer I know.” He could sense that I had something bigger in my life. It was like Duke Ellington. I’m thinking beyond the mundane.
Do you think that is true?
So, when he would tell people that I was a good composer, a good musician, but what I was doing was not commercial at all.
Do think he was right, or not?
